name: Alabaster
lede: Alabaster is the soft, fine-grained white stone used for vases, statues and painters' grounds, and the name of the warm cream that dictionaries have used for its look since the sixteenth century.

sections.title: The stone
sections.body:
Alabaster is a variety of gypsum, hydrated calcium sulfate, and the books describe it as the massive, fine-grained and often banded form [1]. Gypsum takes its name from a Greek word meaning burned, and the clear, translucent form is called selenite [1]. Where the word *alabaster* itself comes from is not covered in our sources.

Trade names confuse the stone. "Oriental alabaster" is banded calcite, not alabaster proper, and "Algerian onyx" is neither alabaster nor onyx [2][3]. Travertine and tufa look much alike but are calcium carbonate [4].

sections.title: The word as a color
sections.body:
As a color word, Paterson defines alabaster as akin to the stone in its whiteness and the smoothness of its texture [5]. He cites Shakespeare's *Richard III*, where it describes the arms of two murdered children [5].

The swatch here is Maerz and Paul's plate 1 A 2 of 1930, which records the name as first used in 1573 [6]. It is a warm cream with a trace of peach, lightness 92 and chroma 15, and its nearest named neighbor is [[ecru]] at a distance of 7.7 [6]. That is warmer than a freshly cut white stone. The swatch is the dictionary's idea of the color, not a measurement of the mineral [5][6].

sections.title: In the painter's studio
sections.body:
Alabaster's main job in painting was hidden. A gesso ground was made of chalk, gypsum or alabaster bound with glue, and Ball and Finlay both list alabaster among the options [7][8]. To make plaster of Paris, either mineral is heated to drive off bound water, and set in glue size the crystals weld together slowly into a hard, smooth surface [7]. Painters used thin gesso, *gesso sottile*, over delicate carving and thick gesso, *gesso grosso*, on flat areas [7].

The records go back several centuries. Pacheco's treatise of 1638 uses a Spanish term for recrystallized calcium sulfate derived from alabaster [2][9]. De Mayerne in 1620 recommended unburnt alabaster as a base for verditer [10]. An English manuscript by Fishwick, written between 1795 and 1816, adds alabaster to paints of quite different colors [2]. The Colour Index of 1971 lists it as a source of Pigment White 25 [2][1]. Finlay says Vermeer made some of his whites with a recipe including alabaster and quartz, a claim we found in that one book only [11].

sections.title: Jars and lamps
sections.body:
Alabaster has long meant a vessel. St Clair notes that ancient Egyptians kept their black eye paint in small jars of alabaster or breccia [12]. In the 1500s Aretino, as Gage reports, pictured the Virgin after the Annunciation filled with light like a lamp in an alabaster vase [13]. The image works because the stone is translucent: it glows when lit from inside [13].

Compare [[ivory]], [[pearl]] and [[white]] for other pale surfaces that carry warmth.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
At least five per cent of the canvas within a color distance of six, the swatch appears in 109 of the 23,781 paintings in our archive, as photographed [14]. It is far more common in some places than others: 34 of the 635 paintings from China, against a much lower rate elsewhere [14]. One painter stands out, [[painter:xugu|Xugu]], with 7 of his 16 paintings in the archive matching, a lift of about 95 times the overall rate [14].

The decade with most matches is the 1780s, 8 of 430 paintings [14]. The colors that keep it company are [[peach]] and [[ecru]] [14]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a look-alike hue and not a pigment test [14].
